questions.question: How did the Bill of Rights impact politics?
questions.solution_html:
• Bill of Rights (1689), signed by William III and Mary II, limited the powers of the
  • monarchy, ended the Divine Right Theory and strengthened Parliament - outlined
  • constitutional and civil liberties - Parliament’s supremacy over the monarchy
  • prohibited the monarch from levying taxes or keeping a standing army without
  • parliamentary consent.

questions.question: What laid the foundation for the two-party system in the political landscape of England?

• Two-party system - the Whigs and the Tories - formalised during the Exclusion Crisis
  • in 1681- on the question of whether James II, a Catholic, should be allowed to become
  • the king of Britain - Whigs opposed James’ succession - Tories supported the
  • hereditary succession.

questions.question: Analyse the contributions of Daniel Defoe to the English novel.
questions.solution_html:
• Eighteenth century - growth of novel as an important literary genre in Britain - Daniel
  • Defoe set the foundation for the modern novel - celebrated for his innovative story telling
  • techniques (first- person narration) and his ability to craft narratives steeped in realism
  • Robinson Crusoe (1719) and Moll Flanders (1722) - stories, designed for a middle-class
  • audience, combined entertainment with moral lessons - significant in the growth of
  • English novels.

questions.question: Examine why Dr. Johnson is celebrated as one of the most influential figures in 18th century literature.
questions.solution_html:
• Samuel Johnson (Dr. Johnson) - critic, poet, essayist, biographer and lexicographer –age
  • referred to as “The Age of Johnson” - early poetic works - “London: A Poem” (1738)
  • and “The Vanity of Human Wishes” (1749) - periodical essays in The Rambler and The
  • Idler - offer reflections on morality, society and literature. A Dictionary of the English
  • Language (1755) - with over 40,000 entries, revolutionised English lexicography
  • included definitions, etymologies and illustrative quotations from various texts (literary
  • philosophical and religious) - philosophical prose works and critical essays like “Preface
  • to Shakespeare” (1765) exhibit his exceptional literary talent. Lives of the Poets (1799
  • 1781) - a ten-volume masterpiece - one of Johnson’s most ambitious works - includes
  • biographical and critical sketches of 52 English poets.

questions.question: Comment on how the colonial and commercial ventures of England set stage for the colonial expansion of England in the future.

  • ambition, military conquest and maritime dominance - Rise of middle class played a
  • significant role in the growth of Britain as an imperial power - top strata of middle class
  • did overseas trading leading to the establishment of British colonies in different parts of
  • the world like in the Americas, Africa, Asia and Pacific - Expansion of transatlantic slave
  • trade - transported millions of enslaved Africans to Caribbean and American plantations
  • - Colonies like Jamaica, Barbados and Antigua - strong economic sources of Britain due
  • to sugar production - British East India Company changed its motives from trade to
  • establishing territorial power in India (after Battle of Plassey and Battle of Buxar)
  • Explorers like James Cook - claimed parts of Australia and New Zealand - Britain’s
  • maritime strength significantly contributed to the emergence of Britain as a major
  • imperial power.

  • ideals: reason, individualism and scientific thinking - influenced the growth of novel - a
  • turn toward realism, everyday life and human experiences - Several factors contributed
  • to the novel’s prominence - invention of printing press, growth of literate middle class
  • and expansion of trade and empire - Influence of Cervantes (Spanish) and Rabelais
  • (French) - Contributions of key figures like Daniel Defoe, Samuel Richardson, Henry
  • Fielding, Tobias Smollett and Laurence Sterne - Role of female novelists like Sarah
  • Fielding and Frances Burney.

questions.question: In what ways did the Whig and Tory factions come to prominence in England?
questions.solution_html:
• Whig and Tory factions rose to political prominence during the late 17th century –
  • particularly around the time of the Exclusion Crisis (1679–1681) - Whigs stood for
  • parliamentary supremacy, religious tolerance for Protestant dissenters, and opposition to
  • arbitrary royal power - represent the interests of the commercial, urban, and more
  • progressive classes.
  • Tories - supported the hereditary right of succession, regardless of religion - loyal to the
  • monarchy and the Anglican Church - drew support from the landed gentry - more
  • conservative in their outlook.
  • Two-party system became more formalized with the Glorious Revolution of 1688 and
  • the establishment of constitutional monarchy - Whigs increasingly dominated politics
  • during Queen Anne’s reign and especially in the early 18th century under the leadership
  • of Robert Walpole, often considered Britain’s first Prime Minister.
  • Rivalry between the Whigs and Tories had a profound impact on literature - rise of the
  • Whigs and Tories marked the beginning of organized party politics in England
  • ideological battles shaped government policy, influenced public opinion, and helped
  • establish the principles of modern parliamentary democracy.
